lines.text: Balloons are in the file too - we shot one down off the Carolinas not long back, nine stories tall with a camera payload, and you know what happened? Everybody knew exactly what it was. It looked like a balloon on radar, it looked like a balloon on video, and when it was over, the file closed with a press conference. That's the difference, counselor. A known intruder gets a report, a shoot-down, and a briefing. An unknown one gets seventy years of calls to my line. If these lights were foreign drones, then Moscow and Beijing have been flying them without transponders over our most sensitive sites for decades - which makes our Air Force the biggest punchline in history - or the lights aren't all drones.

lines.text: Now you're talking like a man who's been in the rooms - and you might be right about the rooms. Careers do hate an unknown. But here's what your own profession taught you: when two rival powers both log the same unexplained thing over their own sensitive sites, in the same decade, in languages that don't share secrets, intelligence doesn't call it the other guy's drone. It calls it a collection failure - and it opens a file. Those files exist on both sides of the Cold War. That isn't geopolitics covering anything up. That's geopolitics being just as confused as everyone else.
